subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage: At a Saturday workshop in a community centre in Indore, Tanvir, a software tester, was handed a sheet titled 'What keeps pulling you?' Vinita, the facilitator, asked everyone to list problems they kept reading about or raising without being asked. Tanvir wrote quickly: village school dropouts, water quality in the old city, and, after a pause, lonely elderly neighbours. Vinita's second question was, 'Which of these fit what you can actually do?' Tanvir crossed out the third, since it needed skills Tanvir didn't have, and circled the first. 'I can build simple tools, and I keep thinking about the school in my grandfather's village.' Vinita asked one more thing: 'Whose voices haven't you heard yet?' Tanvir wrote it as the first line under the circle: talk to the teachers.

qa.q: What was the title of the sheet Tanvir was handed?
qa.a: The sheet was titled 'What keeps pulling you?'

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel about the third problem, and why was it crossed out?
qa.a: Tanvir cared about it, but felt unequipped, since it needed skills Tanvir didn't have.

qa.q: What other approach could Tanvir use to test the first choice?
qa.a: Tanvir could volunteer for a month with a local group working on school dropouts, since real contact shows whether the interest lasts.

qa.q: How might Vinita see Tanvir's choice?
qa.a: Vinita probably sees a sensible one, joining a real concern to real skills, with a first step of listening to teachers.

grounding: Shows a person asking which problems keep drawing their attention and which fit their skills before choosing a purpose project.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage:
Dear Omkar,
You asked what I meant by 'finding my project'. I've been doing an exercise for three weeks, and I think I'm close.
First I wrote down every problem that kept pulling at me, the things I read about at midnight: girls dropping out of school in our district, water tankers in summer, old people alone in flats. Then, next to each, I wrote what I'm actually good at. I'm a data analyst. I'm patient with spreadsheets. I can't dig wells. I don't know teaching.
Where they overlap: school dropout data. The district office publishes it, but nobody reads it. I could help a local NGO spot which villages lose girls after Class 8, and why.
Before I choose, I'm going to call two NGOs next week and ask if that's even useful.
Keerthana

qa.a: Girls dropping out of school in the district, water tankers in summer, and old people alone in flats.

qa.q: How does Keerthana seem to feel about being 'close'?
qa.a: Keerthana feels hopeful and clearer, having found an overlap between a problem that matters and a real skill.

qa.q: Why is calling two NGOs before choosing wise?
qa.a: It checks whether the idea is actually useful to the people doing the work, before Keerthana commits time to it.

qa.q: How might a local NGO see Keerthana's offer?
qa.a: An NGO might welcome free help making sense of data it has no time to read, if it fits the work.

grounding: It shows someone asking which problems keep drawing attention and which fit their skills before choosing a project.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage: Seema, you asked why I'm not joining the tree-planting drive everyone's doing. It's not that I don't care. I'm Urmila, and I spent last month asking myself two questions. One: which problems do I keep coming back to, even when nobody asks me? For me it's clean water in the villages near Nashik, where my grandmother lives, and children who can't read in Class 5. Two: what can I actually do that others can't? I'm a civil engineer. I understand pipes, pumps and tanks. Teaching reading? I'd be a beginner. So water is where my skills meet what I care about. Next month I'm visiting my grandmother's village with a notebook to see what the water committee needs. Trees are good. They're just not my project.

qa.q: Which two problems does Urmila keep coming back to?
qa.a: Clean water in the villages near Nashik and children who can't read in Class 5.

qa.q: How does Urmila feel about not joining the tree-planting drive?
qa.a: Urmila feels calm and sure, caring about the cause but settled that water is where Urmila can help most.

qa.q: Why is visiting the village with a notebook a good next step?
qa.a: It lets Urmila learn what the water committee really needs before designing anything.

qa.q: How might the village water committee see Urmila's visit?
qa.a: They may welcome an engineer who comes to listen first, especially one with family ties to the village.

grounding: It shows someone asking which problems keep drawing attention and which fit their skills, choosing water over causes where they would be a beginner.
